passages.text: Prevention of myopia in a near-primate by supplemental indigo light suggests a hypothesis for the myopia boom
Summary

Today, about 2.8 billion people worldwide suffer from myopia (nearsightedness), and projections place the 2050 burden at 4.8 billion people (the “myopia boom”). <sentence_start/>Myopia results from abnormal elongation of the eye, which causes images to focus in front of the retina. <sentence_start/>Building on prior work in mouse models assessing the non-visual opsin OPN5, we test the hypothesis that insufficient exposure to short-wavelength light increases myopia susceptibility. <sentence_start/>We use the tree shrew, a near-primate model for human myopia. <sentence_start/>Our findings show that indigo light in the range of 419-446 nm, when used to supplement a warm white light-emitting diode (LED), completely suppresses myopia induced by minus-lens wear. <sentence_start/>A large body of genetic and epidemiological evidence suggests that the “myopia boom” has an environmental cause. <sentence_start/>Our findings align with this evidence and suggest that one contributing factor is the relative absence of indigo light in built environments where we spend 86% of our time.
Graphical abstract
Highlights
Indigo light suppresses lens-induced myopia in tree shrews
The most protective wavelength range is 419-446 nm
Tree shrew lens filtering shifts effective OPN5 stimulation to indigo
Built environments may lack protective indigo wavelengths

Grytz et al. show that indigo light supplementation prevents lens-induced myopia in tree shrews. <sentence_start/>The findings suggest that a relative absence of indigo wavelengths in built environments may contribute to the myopia boom and motivate testing indigo-enriched lighting for prevention.
Introduction

The process of establishing perfect focus in the eye is driven by light cues. <sentence_start/>Called emmetropization,<citation rid="bib1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.visres.2024.108402" pmid="38705024" count="1"><sup>1</sup></citation> this developmental progression adjusts the axial length of the eye to ensure that images are focused on the retina. <sentence_start/>The light sensors involved are the opsin class of G protein-coupled receptor.<citation rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2108/zs140094" pmid="25284384" count="1"><sup>2</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Humans have seven opsins implicated in ocular photoreception including the cone (OPN1SW, OPN1MW, and OPN1LW) and rod (OPN2) opsins, as well as the non-canonical opsins OPN3 (encephalopsin), OPN4 (melanopsin), and OPN5 (neuropsin). <sentence_start/>These have photon absorption spectra distributed over the 350-700 nm wavelength range. <sentence_start/>Loss-of-function mutations in mouse models have indicated a role for all opsins in establishing perfect focus: this includes the rod<citation rid="bib3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1167/iovs.14-14648" pmid="25183765" pmcid="PMC4191175" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation> and cone<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.exer.2018.12.021" pmid="30605665" pmcid="PMC6642639" count="1"><sup>4</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.exer.2021.108669" pmid="34126082" count="1"><sup>5</sup></citation> opsins as well as OPN3,<citation rid="bib6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37287644" pmcid="PMC10243678" count="1"><sup>6</sup></citation> OPN4,<citation rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.exer.2021.108866" pmcid="PMC8792255" pmid="34838844" count="1"><sup>7</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciadv.abm9027" pmcid="PMC9176740" pmid="35675393" count="1"><sup>8</sup></citation> and OPN5.<citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2018840118" pmcid="PMC8179197" pmid="34031241" count="1"><sup>9</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>OPN5 is of special interest because it has doi="10.1016/j.ophtha.2016.01.006" pmid="26875007" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This confluence of information has led to the hypothesis<citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" Results
UVA light did not effectively suppress myopia in a near-primate model

Prompted by these findings, we tested the activity of short-wavelength light in the suppression of induced myopia in the tree shrew <italic>Tupaia belangeri</italic>, a small diurnal mammal that is closely related to primates and a model for human myopia.<citation rid="bib22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1167/iovs.64.4.2" pmcid="PMC10080949" pmid="37010856" count="1"><sup>22</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Re-analysis of single-cell sequencing data from tree shrew retina<citation rid="bib23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.34133/research.0536" pmcid="PMC11579486" pmid="39574940" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-023-06638-9" pmid="38092908" pmcid="PMC10719112" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation> indicates that, as might be expected,<citation rid="bib10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1516259112" pmid="26392540" pmcid="PMC4620855" count="1"><sup>10</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41556-019-0301-x" pmid="30936473" pmcid="PMC6573021" count="1"><sup>11</sup></citation> <italic>OPN5</italic> is expressed within cell clusters identified as RGCs according to cell type marker genes (Figure 1). <sentence_start/>Expression of <italic>OPN5</italic> in tree shrew RGCs suggested that UVA light might have an activity in myopia suppression similar to that observed in mice.<citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2018840118" pmcid="PMC8179197" pmid="34031241" count="1"><sup>9</sup></citation><sentence_start/>Figure 1
Expression of <italic>OPN5</italic> in ganglion cells of the tree shrew retina

(A) scRNA-seq UMAPs of retinal cells from the <italic>Tupaia belangeri chinensis</italic> datasets <citation rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-023-06638-9" pmid="38092908" pmcid="PMC10719112" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation> and ,<citation rid="bib23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.34133/research.0536" pmcid="PMC11579486" pmid="39574940" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation> either integrated (top) or individually (lower UMAP plots). <sentence_start/>Color-coding and a retinal lamination schematic depict the photoreceptor (blue), horizontal (yellow), Müller glia (black), bipolar (orange), amacrine (green), ganglionic (red), and “other” (gray) cell classes. <sentence_start/>The retinal ganglion cell (RGC) cluster (red) is at the lower edge of the UMAP plots.

(B) Dot plot depicting the proportion (as a percentage according to the dot size scale) of the cell class (vertical column color-coding as in A) that expresses a class-specific marker gene (named on the horizontal axis), and the average expression level of that gene within the class (greyscale dot shading).

(C) Dot plot depicting the low but detectable expression of <italic>OPN5</italic> (violet dot size and shading scale) across cell class clusters. <sentence_start/>Most <italic>OPN5</italic> expression is found in RGCs (red color-coding and dashed red box). <sentence_start/>The low levels of OPN5 expression found in the amacrine cell clusters (green cluster and dashed green box) may be attributable to nuclear doublets, and the proportion of markers for other cell types detected is shown in the leftmost green dashed box.

To induce myopia in the tree shrew, animals were fitted with spectacles at 24 days after the eyes opened (24 days of visual experience [DVE]) (Figure S1), a juvenile age when they are most susceptible.<citation rid="bib25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0042-6989(98)00053-4" pmid="9893785" count="1"><sup>25</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In experimental animals, the spectacles incorporated a −10 Diopter (D) lens on one side to induce myopia in one eye, while the other eye served as an internal control with no lens. <sentence_start/>Normal control animals were not fitted with spectacles. <sentence_start/>Refraction and axial length were measured every 3 days in fully awake animals (Figure S1A). <sentence_start/>The −10 D lens induced axial elongation, a response that is reliable and reaches a high level of myopia in 35 days.<citation rid="bib22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1167/iovs.64.4.2" pmcid="PMC10080949" pmid="37010856" count="1"><sup>22</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This induced myopia model was intentionally selected because it is a strong myopiagenic stimulus that activates rapid axial elongation at the most susceptible age.

Like humans, tree shrews are typically born hyperopic, with a refractive error larger than 0 D. During normal development, the axial length of the eye slowly increases, actively guided by light stimuli to achieve and then maintain emmetropia (zero refractive error). <sentence_start/>In juvenile animals exposed to standard fluorescent colony lighting (Figure 2A), we observed this normal refractive development from DVE24 to DVE60 in untreated animals (Figure 2B, green trace) and for eyes fitted with spectacles with no lens (Figure 2B, black dashed trace). <sentence_start/>As expected, eyes treated with a −10 D lens developed high levels of myopia by DVE60 (Figure 2B, black trace). <sentence_start/>From DVE24 to DVE60, axial length increased in both normal control animals (Figure 2C, green trace) and in those with spectacles but no lens (Figure 2C, black dashed trace). <sentence_start/>Eyes with a −10 D lens showed accelerated axial elongation over and above the normal elongation rate (Figure 2C, black trace). <sentence_start/>This is an induced myopia.<sentence_start/>Figure 2

For (B), (C), (E), and (F), animals of both sexes were used. <sentence_start/>In (B), (C), (E), and (F), data are presented as mean ± SEM.

To modify the wavelengths of light that tree shrews received during myopia induction, we designed and built ambient lighting units that included a standard “warm white” light-emitting diode (LED) as a primary photon source (Figure S2). <sentence_start/>These are typical of the commoditized 3,000 Kelvin color temperature LEDs used throughout the lighting industry. <sentence_start/>These combine the Nobel Prize- winning<citation rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/anie.201410693" pmid="25411140" count="1"><sup>26</sup></citation> energy-efficient blue LED (typically emitting at 450-460 nm) with layers of phosphors that are excited by blue photons and emit in the green, yellow, and red ranges. <sentence_start/>Switching from fluorescent (Figures 2A-2C) to warm white LED lighting (Figure 2D, warm white LED) did not alter the relative refractive and axial length development of the animals fitted with spectacles, where eyes with a −10 D lens still developed high levels of myopia (Figure 2E, black trace) and accelerated axial elongation (Figure 2F, black trace).

In a first series of experiments, we determined whether LEDs centered at 366 and 395 nm providing supplemental UVA (defined as wavelengths from 315 to 400 nm) (Figure 2D) influenced induced myopia. <sentence_start/>These wavelengths were chosen because they stimulate OPN5 and, based on work performed in the mouse model,<citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2018840118" pmcid="PMC8179197" pmid="34031241" count="1"><sup>9</sup></citation> might be expected to suppress induced myopia. <sentence_start/>In the mouse analysis, UVA light was found to be most effective for myopia suppression if it was delivered for 3 h just before or just after colony lights were turned off. <sentence_start/>This lighting protocol was designed to mimic a natural dusk and recreate the high violet-to-blue wavelength ratio that occurs during nautical twilight (sun angles between −6° and −12°). <sentence_start/>However, because mice are nocturnal animals and dusk is the beginning of their active phase, in the tree shrew analysis described here, we shifted the UVA light exposure to dawn, the beginning of the tree shrew active phase, and exposed for 2 h before and 2 h after the white light was turned on (Figure S1). <sentence_start/>These lighting parameters underscore the role of OPN5 in photoentrainment of the retinal circadian clock<citation rid="bib10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1516259112" pmid="26392540" pmcid="PMC4620855" count="1"><sup>10</sup></citation> and of circadian clock involvement in refractive development.<citation rid="bib27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/opo.12453" pmid="29691928" pmcid="PMC6038122" count="1"><sup>27</sup></citation>

In white LED lighting, control eyes with no lenses showed normal refraction and axial length development (Figures 2E and 2F, black dashed trace). <sentence_start/>Eyes with a −10 D lens showed the expected development of high myopia (Figure 2E, black trace) and exaggerated axial elongation (Figure 2F, black trace). <sentence_start/>UVA light supplementation (Figure 2E, pink trace) did not substantially change the induced myopic refraction (Figure 2E, pink trace) and axial length (Figure 2F, pink trace). <sentence_start/>These findings contrast with the analysis performed in the mouse model where UVA wavelengths effectively suppressed an induced myopia.<citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2018840118" pmcid="PMC8179197" pmid="34031241" count="1"><sup>9</sup></citation>
The tree shrew ocular lens is a UVA prefilter

We considered the possibility that the failure of UVA light to effectively suppress myopia in the tree shrew could be explained by a shift in the absorption spectrum of tree shrew OPN5. <sentence_start/>However, experimental assessment (Figures S3A-S3D) showed that the absorption spectrum peaked at 360-370 nm (Figure 3A), very close to that observed for mice.<citation rid="bib12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M113.514075" pmid="24403072" pmcid="PMC3924266" count="1"><sup>12</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0026388" pmcid="PMC3197025" pmid="22043319" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>We then considered whether the distinct response to UVA in the mouse and tree shrew might be explained by the light transmission characteristics of the ocular lens. <sentence_start/>It has been established that the mouse ocular lens transmits UVA light.<citation rid="bib28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.exer.2009.11.004" pmid="19925789" count="1"><sup>28</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>By contrast, available data suggest that the human lens does not efficiently transmit wavelengths below 400 nm and that there may be progressive absorption of shorter wavelengths with developmental age.<citation rid="bib29" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10375442" doi="10.1006/exer.1999.0687" count="1"><sup>29</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1167/iovs.12-9471" pmid="22491402" count="1"><sup>30</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib31" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>31</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1388-2457(98)00022-4" pmid="10363758" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jcrs.2009.08.035" pmid="20152615" count="1"><sup>33</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0248506" pmcid="PMC7993776" pmid="33764992" count="1"><sup>34</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>To assess the transmission characteristics of the tree shrew lens, we used a wide-spectrum light source and a calibrated spectrometer (Figure S2D). <sentence_start/>Measurements of transmission were conducted immediately after enucleation, using tree shrew lenses, from 10 to 105 days of age. <sentence_start/>This showed (Figure 3A) that as with the human lens, there is a developmental progression in the transmission characteristics. <sentence_start/>The transmission curve changes shape in a complex manner over developmental time, but, in general, wavelengths below 400 nm are transmitted more in younger animals (10 and 24 days of age) (Figure 3A). <sentence_start/>While the lens transmission below 400 nm diminishes in the day 10-30 interval, it increases markedly above 400 nm and remains high thereafter (Figure 3A). <sentence_start/>This means that when the eyelids of tree shrews open at about day 21, the ocular lens transmission profile shifts toward longer wavelengths.<sentence_start/>Figure 3
Tree shrew OPN5 absorption and ocular lens transmission characteristics

(A) Absorption spectrum for OPN5 (black trace and fitted curve) overlaid on the wavelength transmission curves (colored traces) of the tree shrew ocular lens at different ages after birth (10, 24, 30, 45, and 105 days). <sentence_start/>The region of overlap between the OPN5 absorption curve and the lens transmission at 45 days of age is shaded in indigo. <sentence_start/>For wavelength transmission curves, data are presented as the mean ± SEM.

(B) Chart showing the OPN5 absorption curves for mouse (dashed violet line) and tree shrew (dashed blue line), the mouse ocular lens light transmission curve (violet trace), and the lens light transmission curve for juvenile tree shrews averaged at 45 days. <sentence_start/>The colored peaks are the LED output spectra calculated to be optimal for the stimulation of OPN5 in the mouse (purple) and tree shrew (indigo). <sentence_start/>In this analysis, animals of both sexes were used.
(C) Chart showing how the optimal wavelength for stimulation of OPN5 in the tree shrew changed subtly over developmental time.

While the OPN5 absorption spectrum (Figure 3A) was practically identical in mice and tree shrews (Figure 3B, violet and indigo dashed traces), the lens transmission differed substantially (Figure 3B, violet and indigo traces). <sentence_start/>When the absorption curve for OPN5 is overlaid on the ocular lens transmission data (Figure 3A, black trace), it is apparent that stimulation of retinal OPN5 in maturing tree shrews can still be elicited by photons above 400 nm (Figure 3A, indigo shaded region). <sentence_start/>Calculations that take lens prefiltering into account (see STAR Methods) show that the optimal LED peak wavelength for retinal OPN5 stimulation in the mouse versus juvenile tree shrew are distinct (369 nm for mouse and 435 nm for juvenile tree shrew; Figure 3B) and that the optimal wavelength for OPN5 stimulation shifts subtly over developmental time (from 435 to 440 nm; Figure 3C). <sentence_start/>This finding suggested that indigo wavelengths might have the same myopia suppression activity in the tree shrew as UVA wavelengths in the mouse.
Indigo light completely prevents induced myopia in the tree shrew

To test this, we performed additional experiments using warm white LED lighting supplemented with LEDs emitting narrow-band light with peak wavelengths over the 400-468 nm range (Figures 4A-4D and 4G). <sentence_start/>The charts show violet LEDs (400 and 410 nm, Figures 4A-4C) separately but aggregate the data for blue (454 and 468 nm, Figures 4D-4F) and indigo LEDs (421, 432, and 441 nm, Figures 4G-4I). <sentence_start/>Violet wavelengths had a modest, wavelength-dependent effect on suppression of myopia: for 400 nm, myopic refraction shifted from −11.6 D to −8.0 D at DVE60 (Figure 4B) and, for 410 nm, to −5.7 D (Figure 4B). <sentence_start/>Similarly, violet wavelengths suppressed induced axial elongation, such as in the case of 410 nm, to a length that was close to control eyes (Figure 4C). <sentence_start/>Blue wavelength supplementation (Figure 4D) also produced an intermediate suppression effect, with a DVE60 refraction of −6.4 D rather than −11.6D (Figure 4E) and an axial length closer to that of control eyes (Figure 4F). <sentence_start/>By contrast, indigo wavelength supplementation (Figure 4G) completely suppressed refractive change in response to the −10 D lens and produced eyes with a DVE60 refraction of 0.4 D, almost identical to that of controls (Figure 4H, indigo versus dashed trace). <sentence_start/>Indigo wavelength supplementation also eliminated the exaggerated axial elongation of induced myopia and resulted in a slightly reduced axial length change compared with controls throughout the DVE24-60 time course (Figure 4I). <sentence_start/>Indigo light supplementation in these analyses was at 250 μW⋅cm<sup>−2</sup>⋅nm<sup>−1</sup> (4.4 × 10<sup>14</sup> photons⋅cm<sup>−2</sup>⋅sec<sup>−1</sup>), a level designed to elicit a robust biological response. <sentence_start/>However, we also showed that a lower supplementation level of 50 μW⋅cm<sup>−2</sup>⋅nm<sup>−1</sup> (1.0 × 10<sup>14</sup> photons⋅cm<sup>−2</sup>⋅sec<sup>−1</sup>) produced a complete suppression of induced myopia (Figure S4).Figure 4

For all data shown, animals of both sexes were used. <sentence_start/>In (B), (C), (E), (F), (H), (I), and (J), charts show the average measurement at each time point and the standard error as a shaded region. <sentence_start/><italic>p</italic> values are shown on the gray shaded region to the right of the chart, and data are presented as mean ± SEM.

In control eyes with no lens, there was a limited consequence of high-level, short-wavelength light supplementation on either refraction or axial elongation. <sentence_start/>UVA, violet, and blue supplementation resulted in DVE60 refraction of less than 1 D (Figure S5A). <sentence_start/>High-level indigo light, the most effective wavelength for myopia suppression, resulted in a DVE60 refraction of 2.2 D (Figure S5A). <sentence_start/>Similarly, eyes with no lens that received short-wavelength supplementation showed only minor changes in axial length (Figure S5B). <sentence_start/>These effects on the control eye were diminished when using low-level indigo light supplementation (Figures S5C and S5D).

These data show that in a near-primate model of induced myopia, short wavelength light supplementation can completely subvert an aggressive myopiagenic stimulus. <sentence_start/>Expressing refraction and axial length at DVE60 as a measure of efficacy (100% efficacy being complete prevention of abnormal refractive shift or axial length change) against peak wavelengths showed that suppression of myopia with supplemental short-wavelength LED light is exquisitely wavelength sensitive (Figure 4J). <sentence_start/>Notably, the indigo light that provides 100% efficacy in myopia suppression is poorly represented in the spectral power distribution of the fluorescent lights (Figure 2A) and warm white LEDs (Figure 2D) that are mainstays of the lighting industry.

As a means of quantifying the myopia prevention potential of illumination devices and illuminated environments, we developed the μ-opic metric (Figure 4K). <sentence_start/>This metric represents the spectral sensitivity of supplemental short-wavelength light in suppression of myopia. <sentence_start/>The μ-opic was derived empirically from the tree shrew efficacy data obtained in this study and is closely related to the α-opic metrics<citation rid="bib35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12915-024-02038-1" pmid="39538277" pmcid="PMC11562817" count="1"><sup>35</sup></citation> that are used to understand how light affects non-visual responses and as an aid in lighting design. <sentence_start/>Though the μ-opic is defined by myopia suppression activity, it closely follows the shape of the effective OPN5 absorption, as modified by the prefiltering activity of the ocular lens (Figure 4K, compare shaded μ-opic curve with black trace). <sentence_start/>The μ-opic sensitivity spectrum has a slightly asymmetric shape and extends further into the blue compared with the violet and UVA spectra (Figure 4K). <sentence_start/>The upper quartile values of the μ-opic (red numbers in Figure 4K) showed that short wavelengths in the indigo range of 419-446 nm are the most effective supplement for suppressing myopia.

Recent work in the tree shrew shows that narrow-band blue light (in the absence of long wavelengths) can lead to a slow drift toward myopia in otherwise unmanipulated animals.<citation rid="bib64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.visres.2022.108161" pmcid="PMC9974583" pmid="36529048" count="1"><sup>64</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Here, we show that indigo light can suppress induced myopia when used in combination with white light. <sentence_start/>Together, these studies suggest that full-spectrum light may be important for effective myopia suppression. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, indigo light supplementation had a profound effect on eyes with lens-induced high myopia but a small effect on control eyes with no lens. <sentence_start/>This suggests that the effect of indigo light is conditional and most effective when a myopiagenic stimulus is present. <sentence_start/>While high- and low-level indigo light completely suppressed induced myopia, only high-level indigo light could cause a small amount of hyperopia in control eyes. <sentence_start/>Further research is needed to establish light intensities and treatment durations that are effective for myopia suppression without the risk of inducing hyperopia.

Use of the μ-opic metric to assess simulated illuminated environments illustrated the disadvantage of indoor living and the deficiency of warm white LEDs in providing indigo wavelengths for myopia prevention. <sentence_start/>The μ-opic can also be used for designing illuminated environments that deploy the often-preferred warm white light but also provide the proposed myopia prevention benefit of indigo light. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, the μ-opic can be used to guide the incorporation of glazing that transmits shorter-wavelength light with higher efficiency and potentially provides an advantage for myopia prevention. <sentence_start/>We expect that the μ-opic metric will be refined after human studies of indigo light myopia prevention have been completed, but also anticipate, given the high evolutionary conservation between tree shrews and humans, broad opsin absorption spectra, and knowledge of natural sunlight spectra, that more precision in the μ-opic is not essential for effective deployment.

Several testable predictions with translational implications emerge from this study. <sentence_start/>(1) Increasing daytime outdoor exposure is supported as a strategy to reduce myopia; our findings identify indigo light as one candidate component of the outdoor signal. <sentence_start/>(2) Indoor lighting spectra that raise μ-opic exposure in the 419-446 nm band should be evaluated as a practical myopia prevention strategy in children. <sentence_start/>(3) Because short-wavelength-attenuating (“blue-blocking”) spectacles reduce indigo light transmission to the eyes, widespread daytime use in children could plausibly increase the risk of myopia. <sentence_start/>If these hypotheses are confirmed in humans, spectral modifications to built environments could contribute to reducing the growing burden of myopia.<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/519276a" pmid="25788077" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/d41586-024-01518-2" pmid="38811708" count="1"><sup>20</sup></citation>
Limitations of the study

This study demonstrates that indigo light in the range of 419-446 nm could suppress experimentally induced myopia in the tree shrew, a near-primate. <sentence_start/>Though this is a valuable experimental model, it does not fully mimic the natural history of myopia development and progression in humans. <sentence_start/>Studies that directly compare the influence of standard lighting and indigo-supplemented lighting on responses in the human eye are an obvious next step. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, though this study was initiated in response to questions about the function of OPN5 in myopia pathways, it does not directly address the mechanisms that underly this response. <sentence_start/>A comparison of the molecular changes that occur in the tree shrew eye tissues in control eyes and eyes with induced myopia, in standard and indigo-supplemented light, is likely to provide insights into these mechanisms.

under anesthesia a dental acrylic pedestal was surgically installed.<citation rid="bib66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7933981" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>At DVE24, lightweight aluminum spectacles were clipped onto the pedestal.<citation rid="bib66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7933981" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Beforehand, a −10D lens (PMMA, 12 mm diameter, 7.5 mm base curve) was randomly installed into the right or left side of the spectacles while the other side remained open. <sentence_start/>The PMMA lens had a transmittance of 87-93% for wavelengths between 350 nm and 750 nm. <sentence_start/>While the spectacles were fitted to each animal so that the lens was positioned close to the eye, there was a small gap (∼1 mm) between the spectacle frame and the surrounding eye tissues allowing light to reach the eye without passing through the PMMA lens. <sentence_start/>The −10D lens shifts the focal plane behind the retina, which <sentence_start/>These measurements were performed in a darkened room in the morning (around 10 a.m.) and repeated every three days until the experimental endpoint (DVE60). <sentence_start/>Figure S1A Preprocessing

<italic>Tupaia belangeri chinensis</italic> single cell sequencing gene by cell matrices ( <citation rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-023-06638-9" pmid="38092908" pmcid="PMC10719112" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation> & <citation rid="bib23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.34133/research.0536" pmcid="PMC11579486" pmid="39574940" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation>) were downloaded and processed using either a Sketch-based or PCA-integration Seurat (v5) workflow. <sentence_start/>Matrices were merged into a single SeuratObject and subsequently normalized using default parameters for normalization (NormalizeData) and variable feature selection (FindVariableFeatures; features = 2000). <sentence_start/>To integrate the two datasets, we used a sketch-based approach (SketchData; ncells = 5000, method = “LeverageScore”), followed by scaling (ScaleData) and principal component analysis (RunPCA) on the sketch-assay. <sentence_start/>To integrate these layers, we performed integration (IntegrateLayers; k.anchors = 20, dims = 1:30) via reciprocal PCA using as a reference. <sentence_start/>We then performed neighbor analysis (FindNeighbors; reduction = “integrated.pca”, dims = 1:30), clustering (FindClusters; resolution = 2), and dimensionality reduction (RunUMAP; reduction = “integrated.pca”, dims = 1:30). <sentence_start/>Then, the integration and sketch-data were projected onto the non-sketched cells (ProjectIntegration; ProjectData) to identify clusters.

Lighting conditions

All tree shrews were housed in a 14 h/10 h light/dark cycle with the light cycle starting at 6:30 a.m. <sentence_start/>Before the experiment started, all animals were housed in standard fluorescent colony lighting with an approximate illuminance of 400 lx at the bottom of the cage. <sentence_start/>During the experiment, tree shrews were housed individually in cages with dimensions 20″ x 24″ x 35” (width x length x height). <sentence_start/>Tree shrew groups reported in Figures 2B and 2C remained in rooms with standard colony fluorescent lighting throughout the experiment. <sentence_start/>All other groups were housed under controlled lighting conditions using custom light units made from an aluminum frame (Figure S2A). <sentence_start/>Light units consisted of LEDs producing warm white light (3000 K) and narrowband short wavelength light with peak wavelengths at 366 nm, 395 nm, 400 nm, 410 nm, 421 nm, 432 nm, 441 nm, 454 nm, and 468 nm. <sentence_start/>One light unit was placed on top of each cage (Figure S2B) and the light intensity was adjusted to 400 lx warm white light, which was supplemented with short wavelength LED light at 250 μW/cm<sup>2</sup>. <sentence_start/>All light measurements were obtained at the bottom of the cage using a calibrated spectrometer (FLAME-S-UV-VIS-ES, Ocean Optics, Orlando, FL) with a wavelength range of 200-850 nm. <sentence_start/>Attached to the spectrometer was an optical fiber and cosine corrector (CC-3-UV-S, Ocean Optics) pointing upwards toward the light unit during measurements. <sentence_start/>A bi-symmetric log transformation was used for plotting the spectral irradiance of each LED in Figures 2A, 2D, 4A, 4D and G; Figure S5A.<citation rid="bib69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1088/0957-0233/24/2/027001" count="1"><sup>69</sup></citation>

For all short wavelength supplementation shown in Figure 2, narrowband light was used for 4 h in the morning starting at 6:30 a.m. <sentence_start/>To mimic the high content of short wavelengths of dawn, narrowband light was used for 2 h alone followed by 2 h in combination with warm white light. <sentence_start/>Warm white light was used for the remaining 10 h to complete the 14-h light cycle illustrated in Figure S1B. <sentence_start/>Cages with different lighting conditions were housed in separate bays (Figure S2C). <sentence_start/>Each bay was isolated from other light sources by means of blackout curtains. <sentence_start/>Most narrowband LEDs were custom made for this study. <sentence_start/>To allow the replication of our results, the spectral irradiance of each light source can be found in Source Data (sheet “irradiance”). <sentence_start/>For low-level indigo light supplementation (Figure S4) the LEDs employed had a peak output at 421 nm and were used for one hour at dawn, starting at 8 a.m. and finishing at 9 a.m., with warm white light turning on at 8:30 a.m.

Quantification and statistical analysis

Data were analyzed and presented using one of two distinct eye grouping structures: grouping structure A that encompassed various visual conditions, categorized into three subgroups: (i) normal visual experience, −10D lens, and no lens, (ii) different primary light sources (fluorescent and warm white), and (iii) supplemental narrowband LEDs with peak wavelengths of 366 nm, 395 nm, 400 nm, 410 nm, 421 nm, 432 nm, 441 nm, 454 nm, and 468 nm. <sentence_start/>Grouping structure B that was defined by combining the supplemental narrowband LED lights into broader spectral categories: UVA (366 nm, 395 nm), violet (400 nm, 410 nm), indigo (421 nm, 432 nm, 441 nm), and blue (454 nm, 468 nm). <sentence_start/>The left and right eyes of normal subjects showed no significant differences and were thus averaged. <sentence_start/>For longitudinal data analysis, grouping structure B was applied when the longitudinal trends observed in grouping structure A closely overlapped (UVA, indigo, blue), whereas grouping structure A was retained when the trends remained distinct (violet). <sentence_start/>Group differences in longitudinal data were assessed using a hierarchical model-building approach. <sentence_start/>Briefly, a linear mixed-effects model, incorporating linear and quadratic terms and time-group interaction effects, was fitted to the longitudinal data while accounting for correlated measurements. <sentence_start/>The necessity of quadratic terms was evaluated using a likelihood ratio test, which indicated a significant improvement in parameter estimates compared to a model with only linear terms. <sentence_start/>To assess the joint effect of the time-group interaction terms, a Wald chi-square test was conducted to simultaneously evaluate the significance of both the linear and quadratic coefficients on the model’s outcome. <sentence_start/>The treatment efficacy of the different supplemental short-wavelength lights was evaluated using refraction and axial length measurements obtained at the experimental endpoint (60 DVEs). <sentence_start/>Efficacy was calculated separately for refraction and axial length, and the two values were averaged for each eye. <sentence_start/>An efficacy of 0% and 100% corresponded to the average efficacy of eyes of the warm white light group with a −10 D lens and with no lens (control eye), respectively. <sentence_start/>Group differences in treatment efficacy were analyzed using a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) model. <sentence_start/>The fundamental assumptions of the ANOVA model, including normality and homoscedasticity, were verified using the Shapiro-Wilk test and Levene’s test before conducting the analysis. <sentence_start/>Data analysis and visualization were conducted using MATLAB R2021b, while statistical analyses were conducted in R Version 4.3.2, with a significance level of 0.05 applied to all tests.
